cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Due Process Clause requires that a State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before it may permanently terminate parental rights, and New York's fair-preponderance standard was unconstitutional.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.OUT-02: This is the federal constitutional floor that Rhode Island's Family Court applies in every termination case under R.I. Gen. Laws § 15-7-7, and it is the standard the Rhode Island Supreme Court enforces on review.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: A State may not take children from a parent on a presumption of unfitness; every parent, including an unwed father, is entitled to a hearing on fitness before the children are removed, and denying that hearing violates due process and equal protection.
cases.quote: We have concluded that all Illinois parents are constitutionally entitled to a hearing on their fitness before their children are removed from their custody.

relevance.DEC-04: Emergency removal by DCYF is an exception to, not a substitute for, the hearing on fitness this case guarantees, so the exigency justification must be made on the record promptly after the seizure.
relevance.FAIL-05: Stanley is the origin of the rule that a parent may not be stripped of custody because of a status-based classification, which is the analytic starting point for any claim that DCYF acted on a discriminatory presumption.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a child protection agency to protect a child from private violence, so the county's failure to remove Joshua DeShaney from his abusive father was not a constitutional deprivation.
cases.quote: But nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors.

relevance.OUT-06: When a child dies or is seriously injured after DCYF had contact with the family but had not taken custody, DeShaney is the threshold obstacle to any federal damages claim.
relevance.FAIL-04: A First Circuit failure-to-protect claim against DCYF must fit the custody-based 'special relationship' exception DeShaney left open; outside custody there is no federal duty to protect.
relevance.PMC-04: DeShaney explains why fatality review in Rhode Island is a legislative and administrative accountability mechanism rather than a constitutional remedy.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's 'reasonable efforts' requirement, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), creates no right enforceable by foster children either directly or through 42 U.S.C. § 1983.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

relevance.INP-09: Federal oversight of DCYF's intake and investigation performance runs through HHS plan approval and CFSR review, not through private suits, because the plan requirements are not privately enforceable.
relevance.INP-11: Federal funding conditions on child welfare practice, unlike ICWA, generally do not create individually enforceable rights, which is why ICWA claims and IV-E claims are litigated so differently.
relevance.DEC-01: A screen-out or unfounded closure that departs from the federal plan requirements is a compliance matter for HHS rather than a privately actionable federal wrong.
relevance.DEC-06: Prevention and alternative-response obligations under the IV-B/IV-E plan are enforced administratively, so a family denied differential response has no § 1983 claim under the Act.
relevance.ACT-01: The federal reasonable-efforts duty that underlies voluntary service plans is a funding condition, not a private entitlement, so relief must be sought in Family Court.
relevance.OUT-04: Chafee and extended-care obligations are plan requirements of the same character as § 671(a)(15) and are therefore presumptively unenforceable by the youth directly.
relevance.FAIL-03: Suter is the controlling authority on what happens when a state fails federal child welfare standards: the remedy lies with the federal funding agency, not with private plaintiffs.
relevance.PMC-01: CFSR findings are federal administrative findings under an unenforceable plan requirement, which is precisely why published CFSR results carry accountability weight but no private cause of action.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit and fiscal findings under the same IV-E framework are enforced through funding penalties rather than litigation.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen Review Panels are a CAPTA plan condition of the same unenforceable character, so their value is transparency rather than legal remedy.

cases.case_name: Hatch v. Department for Children, Youth & Their Families
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
cases.holding: The Constitution permits a Rhode Island DCYF caseworker to take temporary custody of a child without a hearing when the caseworker has a reasonable suspicion that abuse has occurred or is imminent, and the DCYF worker here met that standard, so qualified immunity barred the claim.
cases.quote: It follows, therefore, that a parent's right to the care, custody, and control of a minor child is inviolate unless a case worker has such a suspicion.

relevance.INP-02: A citizen or professional report is the usual source of the reasonable suspicion that Hatch makes the constitutional trigger for protective custody.
relevance.INP-03: Hatch governs the joint police-DCYF response in Rhode Island: the caseworker's own reasonable suspicion, not police probable cause, is the operative federal standard.
relevance.INP-08: School-sourced reports of injury or disclosure are evaluated against Hatch's reasonable-suspicion threshold before a child may be held.
relevance.INP-10: Hatch rejects any requirement that DCYF complete a full investigation and reach probable cause before escalating to custody.
relevance.INP-12: This is the controlling First Circuit standard for warrantless protective custody of a Rhode Island child.
relevance.DEC-02: Hatch expressly allows DCYF to take custody first and investigate further, framing the acceptance-for-investigation decision.
relevance.DEC-04: Hatch is the case a Rhode Island lawyer must satisfy or defeat on any emergency-removal question in federal court.
relevance.ACT-03: A placement that follows a warrantless removal is constitutionally sound only if the initial seizure met Hatch's reasonable-suspicion test.
relevance.FAIL-02: A removal made without reasonable suspicion of abuse or imminent threat is the unlawful removal Hatch defines and makes actionable under § 1983.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
cases.holding: A parent's familial-integrity right includes the right to prompt post-deprivation process after an emergency separation; the state actor who prolonged the separation without any hearing was not entitled to qualified immunity at summary judgment, while the prosecutor was.
cases.quote: Even when there are such exigent circumstances, there must be an adequate post-deprivation hearing within a reasonable time.

relevance.INP-03: Where law enforcement initiates or prolongs a child's separation from a parent, Suboh imposes the same prompt-hearing duty that applies to DCYF.
relevance.INP-12: Protective custody without a prompt hearing converts a lawful emergency seizure into a continuing due process violation.
relevance.DEC-04: Suboh supplies the procedural half of the removal analysis that Hatch leaves open: exigency justifies the taking, but not the keeping.
relevance.ACT-05: Interim orders restricting contact must themselves be reviewable promptly; an unreviewed no-contact posture is the defect Suboh condemns.
relevance.FAIL-02: Failure to provide a timely post-removal hearing is an independently actionable § 1983 violation in the First Circuit.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
cases.holding: Dismissal of § 1983 and state claims against counselors whose abuse report led to removal was affirmed: the familial-integrity interest is not absolute, testimony in the child protection proceeding carried absolute witness immunity, and the state reporting statute immunized the good-faith report even if the underlying counseling was negligent.
cases.quote: While the Supreme Court has recognized an abstract fundamental liberty interest in "family integrity," the Court has never found that interest to be absolute or unqualified.

relevance.INP-01: Watterson holds that a mandated reporter's good-faith report is immunized even where the professional work producing it is alleged to have been negligent.
relevance.INP-02: The same reporting immunity protects non-mandated participants in the child protection process in the First Circuit.
relevance.INP-04: Court-appointed evaluators who report and testify in an abuse proceeding enjoy absolute witness immunity for that testimony.
relevance.INP-06: A hotline or third-party report made in good faith does not expose the reporter to damages liability even if the resulting removal was wrong.
relevance.INP-08: School and clinical personnel who report suspected abuse are protected on the same reasoning.
relevance.FAIL-02: Watterson is the standard defense answer to a wrongful-removal damages theory built on the reporter rather than the removing agency.

cases.case_name: Carter ex rel. Caleb O. v. Lindgren
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
cases.holding: Summary judgment for Rhode Island DCYF officers was affirmed because, applying Hatch, the officers had an objectively reasonable suspicion of abuse when they took the children into temporary custody, so no constitutional violation occurred.
cases.quote: We need not address the latter two aspects of the Hatch test because we conclude that plaintiffs have not established a constitutional violation.

relevance.INP-03: Carter shows how the Hatch test is applied to a Rhode Island DCYF response triggered by a criminal investigation of a parent.
relevance.DEC-04: This is the leading First Circuit application of Hatch to an actual DCYF emergency removal decision.
relevance.FAIL-02: Carter demonstrates that a later Family Court reunification order does not retroactively make the original DCYF removal unconstitutional.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
cases.holding: Rhode Island DCYF social workers were entitled to qualified immunity on substantive due process claims by twins abused in foster care because the evidence did not show conscience-shocking conduct, and Rhode Island sovereign and qualified immunity barred the state negligence claims.
cases.quote: state officials must have been at least aware of known or likely injuries or abuse and have chosen to ignore the danger to the child

relevance.ACT-03: This case defines what a Rhode Island foster placement must look like before a caseworker's monitoring failures become constitutionally actionable.
relevance.OUT-06: Serious injury to a child in DCYF foster care does not itself establish liability; the plaintiff must prove the workers knew of and ignored the danger.
relevance.FAIL-04: J.R. v. Gloria is the controlling Rhode Island authority on § 1983 claims for harm suffered under agency supervision, and it also confirms state sovereign and qualified immunity defenses.
relevance.PMC-04: The opinion documents the evidentiary gap that routinely defeats post-harm accountability suits and that fatality and near-fatality review is meant to close.

cases.case_name: Sam M. ex rel. Elliott v. Carcieri
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
cases.holding: The district court abused its discretion in refusing to let the proposed next friends represent children in DCYF custody and in dismissing their systemic class action; the complaint was reinstated and the next friends appointed.
cases.quote: We remand the case with directions to reinstate the complaint and allow Ms. Melvin, Ms. Collins, and Dr. Elliott to proceed as the children's Next Friends.

relevance.INP-09: Sam M. is the procedural gateway through which systemic challenges to Rhode Island's child welfare system reach federal court.
relevance.ACT-03: The class was defined as all children in DCYF legal custody due to a report or suspicion of abuse or neglect, making this the vehicle for challenging placement practice as a whole.
relevance.OUT-04: Youth aging out of DCYF custody fall within the certified class definition and can be represented through next friends rather than having to sue individually.
relevance.FAIL-03: Systemic failure claims against DCYF proceed as next-friend class actions because the federal plan requirements are not individually enforceable.
relevance.PMC-01: Class litigation of this kind is the practical counterpart to CFSR monitoring when federal review alone does not produce change.
relevance.PMC-02: The opinion shows how independent representation, rather than agency self-reporting, surfaces facts about agency performance.
relevance.PMC-03: The Rhode Island Child Advocate's support for the next friends illustrates the role independent review bodies play in child welfare accountability.
relevance.PMC-06: Sam M. establishes that third parties without a prior custodial relationship may stand up for children in DCYF custody, which is the legal basis for outside analysis and advocacy.

cases.case_name: Danny B. ex rel. Elliott v. Raimondo
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
cases.holding: In the Rhode Island foster care class action, the district court abused its discretion by completely barring the plaintiff foster children from communicating with their own lawyers before trial, and the resulting prejudice required reversal.
cases.quote: We hold, therefore, that the court below abused its discretion when it completely denied the plaintiffs access to their lawyers prior to trial.

relevance.INP-09: Danny B. is the second generation of systemic oversight litigation over DCYF and shows how such cases are actually tried.
relevance.OUT-04: Older youth in DCYF custody have their own attorney-client relationship in systemic litigation that the state may not sever.
relevance.FAIL-03: This is the leading recent First Circuit decision on litigating Rhode Island's child welfare system-wide performance.
relevance.PMC-01: It illustrates the judicial oversight track that operates alongside federal CFSR monitoring.
relevance.PMC-03: The decision protects the independence of the children's own representation from state control.
relevance.PMC-06: Danny B. confirms that children in DCYF custody retain independent access to counsel and advocates, the precondition for outside accountability work.

cases.case_name: Curtis v. State Department for Children & Their Families
cases.holding: Directed verdicts for a school social worker, a DCF protective worker, a hospital and a physician were affirmed: the school worker was required to report under § 40-11-3, the physician's three-day hospital hold was authorized by § 40-11-5, and no false imprisonment, battery or emotional distress claim was proved.
cases.quote: Any physical injury apparently caused by other than accidental means is sufficient under § 40-11-5.

relevance.INP-01: Curtis is the Rhode Island Supreme Court's fullest treatment of the § 40-11-3 reporting duty and of liability exposure for making a report.
relevance.INP-02: The Court reads § 40-11-3 as imposing the reporting duty on any person with reasonable cause to know or suspect abuse, not only on listed professionals.
relevance.INP-06: A report based on second-hand information from teachers was held more than sufficient to mandate a report, which sets a low threshold for hotline intake.
relevance.INP-07: The case sets the standard for a physician's statutory authority to hold an apparently injured child for up to seventy-two hours.
relevance.INP-08: School personnel who relay a child's disclosure of a beating trigger the mandatory report; the school social worker acted lawfully in doing so.
relevance.INP-12: Curtis is the Rhode Island authority for medically initiated protective custody without parental consent.
relevance.DEC-01: Because the reporting and hold thresholds are so low, the substantive filtering in Rhode Island occurs at investigation and adjudication rather than at intake.
relevance.DEC-02: Section 40-11-3 requires the department to cause a non-physician report to be investigated immediately and to have the child examined by a licensed physician.
relevance.ACT-06: The physician's seventy-two-hour hold under § 40-11-5 is the statutory basis for emergency medical custody in Rhode Island.

cases.holding: Affirming termination, the Court set out the ex parte petition, preliminary hearing and probable-cause hearing sequence under § 40-11-7.1 and held that the twelve-month period for termination may run from the child's placement in DCYF care rather than from a formal finding of abuse or neglect.
cases.quote: Next, a hearing on the petition must be held within seven days.

relevance.INP-04: This opinion maps the Family Court's role from the ex parte petition forward, including the interim orders a judge may make.
relevance.INP-10: It explains the statutory escalation from DCYF's ex parte filing to preliminary and probable-cause hearings.
relevance.INP-12: Christina V. sets the Rhode Island timetable that converts an emergency detention order into a reviewable judicial proceeding.
relevance.DEC-04: The seven-day preliminary hearing is the state-law deadline that follows any ex parte removal order.
relevance.DEC-05: This is the Rhode Island Supreme Court's clearest description of what filing an abuse or neglect petition sets in motion.
relevance.ACT-05: The Family Court is authorized to make interim orders in its discretion respecting the rights of the child pending the probable-cause hearing.

cases.holding: Certiorari was denied to a clinical social worker resisting a grand jury subpoena for counseling records, because § 5-37.3-6.1 requires that the patient receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before process issues and the confidentiality questions can be fully litigated in the Superior Court.
cases.quote: Glatter's patient also must be afforded notice and an opportunity to be heard before process may issue for any confidential health care information.

relevance.INP-07: Counseling and health care records generated in a child abuse context are confidential and reachable only through the statutory notice-and-challenge procedure.
relevance.ACT-06: Therapeutic records created during court-ordered or emergency psychological care carry a statutory presumption of confidentiality.
relevance.FAIL-06: The decision shows that the remedy for improper disclosure of protected records is judicial, and that the presumption runs in favor of privacy.
relevance.PMC-05: Any transparency request touching health care communications must accommodate the individual's right to notice and to contest disclosure.

cases.holding: A parent who discharges appointed counsel in a termination proceeding has no right to have substitute counsel appointed, and the trial justice did not err in proceeding after the mother dismissed her attorney.
cases.quote: For all the foregoing reasons, we hold that the trial justice was not obligated to appoint substitute counsel after respondent discharged her appointed counsel.

relevance.FAIL-01: Bryce T. is the Rhode Island authority defining the limits of the appointed-counsel right in termination cases and is the case most often invoked when a parent seeks reversal for lack of representation.

cases.holding: The Court vacated the portion of the termination decree resting on the mother's mental deficiency under § 15-7-7(a)(2)(i) for lack of legally competent evidence, affirmed unfitness on another ground, and quashed as moot DCYF's certiorari petition about ending visitation pending appeal.
cases.quote: Reversing the Family Court's decision to terminate Mary Ann's parental rights pursuant to § 15-7-7(a)(2)(i) (mental deficiency), we vacate that portion of the TPR decree.

relevance.ACT-02: The opinion describes the enhanced supervised visitation and parenting services DCYF must actually deliver before relying on a parent's failure to benefit.
relevance.ACT-05: It addresses the Family Court's suspension of a parent's visitation privileges on DCYF's motion, the mechanism by which contact is restricted short of removal.
relevance.OUT-05: Christopher B. shows the Rhode Island Supreme Court vacating a statutory ground that the record did not support, leaving that theory dismissed.
relevance.FAIL-05: This is the leading Rhode Island case policing the use of a parent's mental deficiency as a termination ground, and it insists on legally competent evidence rather than inference from disability.

cases.holding: The termination decree was affirmed, but the Court held that the child's statement to his foster mother was not made within a reasonable time after the alleged abuse and so fell outside the relaxed hearsay standard for children's statements in Family Court proceedings.
cases.quote: In light of the circumstances of this case, we conclude that Alexis's statement to his foster mother was not made within a reasonable time after the alleged abuse.

relevance.DEC-02: Alexis L. governs when a child's out-of-court disclosure gathered during an investigation may actually be used as evidence, and it sets real limits on the relaxed standard for children's statements.
relevance.DEC-03: A substantiated finding that rests on a delayed child disclosure is vulnerable if the statement does not satisfy the timeliness requirement.

cases.holding: The dependency decree was vacated and a new trial ordered because DCYF committed an Indian child to foster placement without the qualified expert witness testimony ICWA requires and without the finding that placement with the father would likely cause serious emotional or physical damage.
cases.quote: In light of such disregard of ICWA requirements, we cannot say that the error was harmless.

relevance.INP-11: Tamika R. is the leading Rhode Island Supreme Court decision applying ICWA and holding that its qualified-expert-witness requirement is not excused by a social worker's testimony.
relevance.DEC-05: A dependency petition involving an Indian child cannot be adjudicated on the ordinary state record; the ICWA evidentiary requirements attach from the outset.
relevance.ACT-03: Foster placement of an Indian child without the ICWA findings is reversible error, not harmless.
relevance.ACT-04: The Court faulted DCYF for bypassing a willing father and his household, applying ICWA's skepticism of removal based on poverty or non-conforming behavior.
relevance.OUT-05: The decree was vacated outright, showing that ICWA non-compliance can undo an entire dependency adjudication.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is the clearest Rhode Island example of an appellate court reversing an agency-driven adjudication for statutory non-compliance.
relevance.FAIL-03: Tamika R. documents an admitted state failure to meet a federal child welfare mandate in an individual case.
relevance.FAIL-05: The Court invoked the ICWA guideline that poverty, inadequate housing or non-conforming social behavior alone cannot support removal, a direct check on culturally biased decision-making.

cases.holding: Termination on abandonment and desertion grounds was affirmed where the father expressed no interest in reunification and had no contact for the statutory six-month period, and the best-interests finding was supported by legally competent evidence.
cases.quote: Therefore, the trial justice's finding that termination was in the best interests of the children is supported by legally competent evidence, and we decline to disturb this finding on appeal.

relevance.INP-05: A parent's stated lack of interest in reunification, recorded at the service-planning stage, later becomes evidence of abandonment.
relevance.ACT-01: The case shows how a parent's refusal to engage with offered services is documented and used.
relevance.ACT-04: The children's stability in their existing foster placement was central to the best-interests determination, which is how placement quality enters the permanency analysis.
relevance.OUT-03: Daniel D. states the Rhode Island best-interests standard that governs whichever permanency outcome the Family Court selects.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination, reiterating that a finding of parental unfitness is a mandatory predicate that must precede any termination of parental rights.
cases.quote: A trial justice must make a finding of unfitness before she may terminate a parent's rights.

relevance.OUT-02: This is the cleanest Rhode Island statement of the unfitness-first rule: best interests never substitute for a finding of unfitness in a termination case.

cases.holding: Termination was affirmed and no due process violation occurred where the incarcerated father participated by telephone and, even after the line dropped during the bench decision, his attorney actively represented him throughout.
cases.quote: As such, we are satisfied that no due-process violation occurred in this case.

relevance.DEC-05: Julian D. governs how a Rhode Island dependency or termination case proceeds when a parent cannot be physically present, and it makes active representation by counsel the due process safeguard.

cases.holding: Termination of the father's rights to his surviving son was affirmed on the cruel-or-abusive-conduct ground after clear and convincing evidence showed he was the sole caretaker when his five-week-old daughter sustained the fatal non-accidental injuries.
cases.quote: the statute dictates that "the department has no obligation to engage in reasonable efforts to preserve and reunify a family."

relevance.INP-07: Medical evidence that injuries were non-accidental and untreated supplied both the abuse finding and the neglect finding for failure to seek care.
relevance.ACT-06: The father's failure to obtain medical treatment for the injured infant was itself held to constitute neglect and cruel and abusive conduct.
relevance.OUT-06: This is the Rhode Island decision showing how a child fatality is used to terminate rights to a surviving sibling.
relevance.FAIL-04: It establishes that cruel or abusive conduct toward any child relieves DCYF of the reasonable-efforts duty as to the remaining children.
relevance.PMC-04: The opinion documents the pattern of repeated non-accidental injuries over weeks that fatality review exists to detect earlier.

cases.holding: Because the criminal convictions and life sentences on which the unfitness finding principally rested were vacated while the appeal was pending, the termination decree was vacated and the case remanded for further proceedings.
cases.quote: we vacate the decree terminating the respondent's parental rights with respect to Izabella and remand this case to the Family Court for further proceedings as expeditiously as practicable

relevance.ACT-04: The father's preference that the child be placed with his mother rather than the foster parent frames the kinship question in a Rhode Island permanency record.
relevance.OUT-03: The competing adoption and relative-placement options in the case show how Rhode Island courts choose among permanency paths.
relevance.OUT-05: The decree was set aside entirely, returning the case to the Family Court rather than closing it.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is the Rhode Island example of a termination collapsing when the conviction underlying the incarceration ground is vacated on Fourth Amendment grounds.

cases.holding: Dependency decrees as to both children were affirmed, and the Court held that evidence of harm to the first child was properly considered in determining the dependency of the second.
cases.quote: Thus, we are of the opinion that the trial justice's finding of dependency as to King is supported by clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.DEC-03: King J. confirms that harm to one child is competent evidence bearing on the status of a sibling, which is how Rhode Island substantiations spread across a household.
relevance.DEC-05: The case shows a dependency petition filed and adjudicated as to multiple siblings on a shared evidentiary record.

cases.case_name: Providence Journal Co. v. Rhode Island Department of Public Safety
cases.holding: Denial of the newspaper's Access to Public Records Act request for state police investigative records was affirmed because the subject's substantial privacy interest outweighed the asserted public interest, and a bare assertion of possible government impropriety does not compel disclosure.
cases.quote: Pursuant to the APRA, records need not be disclosed where such disclosure could create an unwarranted invasion of privacy

relevance.FAIL-06: This decision sets the Rhode Island balancing test that determines whether a transparency failure is unlawful or a lawful privacy withholding.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the controlling Rhode Island authority on the privacy exemption that most often blocks release of child-welfare-adjacent investigative records.
relevance.PMC-06: The Court required more than speculation about official impropriety to tip the balance toward disclosure, which sets the evidentiary bar for public accountability requests.

cases.holding: A neglect decree against an incarcerated father was affirmed; findings of dependency and neglect must be made by clear and convincing evidence under Rule 17(b), and the father's inability to care for the child during an eighteen-month sentence supported the finding despite his financial provision for the household.
cases.quote: Based upon our review of the record, we are of the opinion that legally competent evidence exists to support the trial justice's findings of neglect.

relevance.DEC-03: Kurt H. states the clear-and-convincing standard and the definitions of neglect under both chapter 1 of title 14 and chapter 11 of title 40 that control a Rhode Island substantiation.
relevance.DEC-05: The opinion traces an ex parte petition through temporary custody to a contested neglect adjudication.
relevance.ACT-03: It shows commitment to DCYF care, custody and control following a neglect finding against an incarcerated parent.

cases.holding: Termination was affirmed on the abandonment ground because the father, who had the Family Court and DCYF addresses and was represented by counsel elsewhere, failed to maintain contact, so the Court did not need to reach the alternative unfitness ground.
cases.quote: Because we are of the opinion that the Family Court justice correctly concluded that respondent abandoned his son, we need not address § 15-7-7(a)(2)(i) as an additional basis for termination.

relevance.INP-06: The case began with a hotline call describing the incident, illustrating how an anonymous or third-party report opens a DCYF file that can end in termination.
relevance.OUT-02: Malachii O. is the modern Rhode Island statement of the abandonment ground and confirms that one sustained statutory ground is enough to affirm.

cases.holding: The father's challenge to the adoption petition's failure to specify statutory grounds was waived because he never objected below, and his rights were properly terminated on the abandonment ground under § 15-7-7(a)(4).
cases.quote: Accordingly, it is our view that respondent's first contention on appeal has been waived.

relevance.OUT-03: Kyeshon J. is the Rhode Island authority for terminating a parent's rights inside an adoption proceeding, the route by which many kinship and caregiver permanency plans are finalized, and it shows that objections not raised in Family Court are lost.

cases.case_name: Pontarelli v. Rhode Island Department of Elementary & Secondary Education
cases.holding: The requested records fell within an APRA exception and were not public records, so the agency's denial was upheld; separately, any reason not stated in the denial is deemed waived absent good cause.
cases.quote: we hold without hesitation that the records Pontarelli requested are not public records for the purposes of APRA

relevance.FAIL-06: Pontarelli defines how Rhode Island courts decide whether withheld agency records were ever 'public records' at all, the first question in any disclosure-failure claim.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit-adjacent personnel and investigative material held by a state agency may fall outside APRA entirely.
relevance.PMC-05: The waiver rule under § 38-2-7(a) is the practical lever a requester has: reasons omitted from the denial letter are generally forfeited.

cases.holding: Abuse and neglect findings were affirmed on medical evidence of fourteen non-accidental fractures, and the mother's Fourteenth Amendment challenge to DCYF's seventy-two-hour hold was not preserved because the parents waived the Rule 15(c)(5) probable-cause hearing.
cases.quote: Therefore, we conclude that Kimberly's challenge to the temporary hold on the children was not preserved for appeal.

relevance.INP-04: The opinion shows the ex parte petition and probable-cause hearing machinery operating after a hospital-initiated referral.
relevance.INP-10: It confirms that a seventy-two-hour hold escalates into a judicial proceeding at which the parent must act to preserve objections.
relevance.INP-12: Madlyn B. is the Rhode Island case that tells parents' counsel exactly when to contest a protective hold.
relevance.DEC-03: The substantiation rested on the trial justice's inference that the primary caregiver either inflicted or allowed the abuse.
relevance.DEC-04: A constitutional challenge to an emergency hold must be raised at the probable-cause hearing or it is waived.
relevance.OUT-06: Serious non-accidental injury to an infant is the fact pattern that drives both the hold and the adjudication here.
relevance.FAIL-02: This is the single most important Rhode Island practice point on unlawful-removal claims: waiving the probable-cause hearing forfeits the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment challenge.

cases.holding: On remand after the earlier vacatur, termination was affirmed; the Court restated that findings in a termination proceeding must rest on clear and convincing evidence and upheld admission of the child's statements to her therapist under Rule 803(4).
cases.quote: Such findings must be supported by clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.DEC-03: The decision governs the admissibility of a child's statements made to a therapist for treatment, a recurring evidentiary basis for Rhode Island abuse findings.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the current Rhode Island Supreme Court statement of the burden of proof and standard of review in termination appeals.

cases.holding: The abuse and neglect decree against the mother was vacated because the evidence did not clearly and convincingly show that she inflicted or allowed the infant's injuries, where she reported the bruising immediately and followed medical advice.
cases.quote: We are of the opinion, therefore, that Anna's response to discovering the bruising, even if arguably dilatory, does not support a finding of abuse or neglect.

relevance.INP-01: The case arises from a pediatric report of unexplained infant bruising and shows how a medical referral becomes a DCYF petition.
relevance.INP-07: Child-abuse pediatrician testimony was the core evidence, and the Court scrutinized how far it could carry a finding against a non-inflicting parent.
relevance.INP-10: It shows an intake escalating to an eleven-day abuse and neglect trial on medical evidence alone.
relevance.DEC-01: Sophia M. is the Rhode Island decision that marks where the evidence runs out and a case should not be founded against a parent.
relevance.DEC-02: The opinion criticizes reliance on an impermissible pyramid of inferences drawn from an investigation.
relevance.DEC-03: It is the controlling limit on substantiating a non-perpetrating parent under the 'allowed to be inflicted' theory.
relevance.OUT-01: The Court expressly warned that a pending appeal should not delay reunification efforts where reunification is in the child's best interest.
relevance.OUT-05: The decree was vacated as to the mother, the paradigm of a Rhode Island case dismissed for insufficient evidence.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is the leading recent example of the Rhode Island Supreme Court reversing a DCYF-obtained abuse and neglect finding.

cases.holding: The termination decree was vacated and remanded for a hearing with proper notice because the record did not show compliance with § 15-7-9, which requires a sworn affidavit of the absent parent's last known whereabouts before notice by publication may be ordered.
cases.quote: Our examination of the record, however, reveals a fatal flaw in this case which constrains us to vacate the termination decree.

relevance.OUT-02: Joziah B. makes § 15-7-9 notice a strict prerequisite to any Rhode Island termination against an absent parent.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the clearest recent instance of a Rhode Island termination being undone for a notice defect the parties themselves had not fully briefed.

cases.holding: Termination was affirmed where DCYF developed four case plans tailored to the mother's issues and the Family Court correctly concluded the department satisfied its statutory reasonable-efforts obligation notwithstanding her non-compliance.
cases.quote: we are of the opinion that the Family Court justice correctly concluded that DCYF complied with its statutory obligation to make reasonable efforts to reunify respondent with Violet

relevance.INP-05: A parent's refusal to acknowledge a mental-health issue affecting parenting capacity is treated as non-compliance rather than as a need the department failed to address.
relevance.DEC-06: The case shows that repeated tailored planning, not a single offer of services, is what satisfies the statutory duty.
relevance.ACT-01: Violet G. defines what a carefully tailored Rhode Island case plan must contain to count as a reasonable effort.
relevance.ACT-02: It is the leading recent Rhode Island authority on the reasonable-efforts finding in court-ordered case planning.
relevance.OUT-01: Two years of unsuccessful visitation and the absence of a maternal bond supported the conclusion that safe return was not substantially probable.
relevance.OUT-02: The opinion ties the reasonable-efforts finding directly to the § 15-7-7(a)(3) twelve-month and substantial-probability analysis.

cases.holding: Termination was affirmed over an ineffective-assistance and right-to-counsel challenge because the parent knowingly chose to proceed pro se after his attorney withdrew, the trial justice canvassed the risks, and stand-by counsel was appointed.
cases.quote: Considering the entire record, it is evident that respondent has failed to allege any basis for a finding that he did not knowingly give up his right to counsel.

relevance.FAIL-01: Mandy M. is the current Rhode Island framework for ineffective-assistance and waiver-of-counsel claims in termination appeals, including the Rule 18 appointment duty and the stand-by counsel practice.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Servs. of Durham Cty.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Due Process Clause does not categorically require appointed counsel for an indigent parent in a termination proceeding; the question is answered case by case by the trial court under the Mathews v. Eldridge factors, and no counsel was required on this record.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.FAIL-01: Lassiter is the federal decision under which In re Bryce T. and In re Mandy M. operate, and it is the first authority a Rhode Island parent claiming reversal for lack of counsel must confront, because it establishes that the right is case-specific rather than automatic.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: A section 1983 plaintiff must identify the particular statutory provision said to confer an individual federal right; Title IV-D's 'substantial compliance' requirement is only a systemwide yardstick for the Secretary and confers no such right, so the judgment was vacated for provision-by-provision analysis.
cases.quote: In order to seek redress through § 1983, however, a plaintiff must assert the violation of a federal right, not merely a violation of federal law.

relevance.INP-09: Blessing explains why a systemic challenge to DCYF intake and investigation performance cannot be pleaded as a blanket right to 'substantial compliance' with the federal plan and must instead be tied to a specific rights-creating provision.
relevance.DEC-01: A screen-out that departs from federal plan requirements fails the Blessing test because compliance standards of that kind are yardsticks for the federal auditor rather than entitlements of the reported child.
relevance.PMC-01: CFSR performance measures are precisely the kind of aggregate, audit-triggering standard Blessing holds to be unenforceable by individuals, which is why CFSR results are accountability data rather than a cause of action.
relevance.PMC-02: Blessing describes the funding-reduction mechanism as the enforcement tool for plan noncompliance, which is the same fiscal-penalty track that governs IV-E audit findings against Rhode Island.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Reversing, the Court held that a federal spending statute creates a section 1983-enforceable right only when it unambiguously confers one in individually focused, rights-creating terms, and FERPA's nondisclosure provisions, which speak to the Secretary of Education, do not.
cases.quote: We now reject the notion that our cases permit anything short of an unambiguously conferred right to support a cause of action brought under §1983.

relevance.DEC-06: Differential-response and prevention obligations in the IV-B/IV-E plan are directed to the agency and the Secretary rather than phrased in terms of the family benefited, so under Gonzaga they confer no individually enforceable right.
relevance.OUT-04: Chafee and extended-care plan requirements must be tested against Gonzaga's rights-creating-language standard before a Rhode Island youth can sue over them, rather than assumed unenforceable on Suter's broader reasoning alone.
relevance.FAIL-03: Gonzaga supplies the test that now decides whether a Rhode Island failure to meet a federal child welfare standard is privately actionable at all, replacing the looser 'zone of interest' reading some courts drew from Blessing.
relevance.PMC-03: CAPTA's Citizen Review Panel condition is addressed to the state plan and not to any identified class of beneficiaries, so Gonzaga confirms that panels operate as transparency bodies rather than as a source of enforceable rights.

cases.case_name: Health and Hospital Corporation of Marion Cty. v. Talevski
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Spending Clause statutes can create rights enforceable under section 1983; the Federal Nursing Home Reform Act's unnecessary-restraint and predischarge-notice provisions unambiguously confer individual rights, and the Act's own enforcement scheme does not foreclose a section 1983 suit, so the judgment for the resident was affirmed.
cases.quote: our precedent sets a demanding bar: Statutory provisions must unambiguously confer individual federal rights.

relevance.INP-09: Talevski is the current framework for deciding whether any federal child welfare plan requirement bearing on DCYF intake performance is privately enforceable, and it forecloses treating Suter as a categorical bar on Spending Clause claims.
relevance.INP-11: Because ICWA claims and Title IV-E claims are litigated so differently, counsel must run each asserted federal right through Talevski's two-step inquiry rather than assuming the funding-condition label resolves enforceability.
relevance.DEC-01: A federal challenge to Rhode Island's screening or unfounded-closure practice survives only if the specific plan provision invoked clears Talevski's demanding unambiguous-conferral bar.
relevance.DEC-06: Prevention and alternative-response obligations must be tested provision by provision under Talevski; the modern question is whether the text is individual-centric, not whether the statute is Spending Clause legislation.
relevance.ACT-01: The reasonable-efforts duty behind a Rhode Island voluntary service plan is still most naturally enforced in Family Court, but Talevski requires that conclusion to be reached through its unambiguous-conferral analysis rather than by citing Suter alone.
relevance.OUT-04: Talevski is the decision a Rhode Island youth aging out of DCYF custody would invoke to argue that a particular Chafee or extended-care provision is individually focused enough to be enforceable.
relevance.FAIL-03: Talevski is the controlling modern statement of when a state's failure to meet a federal child welfare standard can be remedied by a private suit rather than only by federal funding action.
relevance.PMC-01: It confirms that the unenforceability of CFSR-measured plan standards rests on the particular text of those provisions, not on a blanket rule about Spending Clause programs.
relevance.PMC-02: Talevski leaves fiscal and audit conditions enforced through funding penalties while preserving private enforcement for provisions that are genuinely rights-creating.
relevance.PMC-03: The CAPTA Citizen Review Panel condition must be analyzed under Talevski before anyone concludes that panel obligations are unenforceable, even though the text points strongly that way.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Reversing, the Court held that ICWA section 1912(f) does not apply where the Indian parent never had custody, that section 1912(d) active-efforts remedial services are not required where the parent abandoned the child before birth and never had custody, and that section 1915(a) preferences do not apply where no preferred party has sought to adopt.
cases.quote: As a result, § 1912(f) does not apply in cases where the Indian parent never had custody of the Indian child.

relevance.INP-11: This is the Supreme Court's construction of the two ICWA provisions Rhode Island litigated in In re Roman A., and it is the authority that defines when the heightened 'continued custody' and 'active efforts' protections attach to a non-custodial Indian parent.
relevance.ACT-04: The Court held that ICWA's extended-family and tribal placement preferences under section 1915(a) do not displace an existing placement when no preferred relative or tribal family has formally come forward to adopt, which is the federal limit on the kinship-preference argument.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court upheld ICWA against Article I and anticommandeering challenges and dismissed the equal protection and nondelegation challenges to the placement preferences for lack of standing, leaving the statute intact.
cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

relevance.INP-11: Brackeen confirms that ICWA remains fully operative federal law binding on Rhode Island's Family Court, which a 2026 brief must state rather than leaving the reader with only two Rhode Island ICWA decisions from 2009 and 2019.
relevance.ACT-04: The placement preferences that drive ICWA kinship and tribal placement in Rhode Island survived this challenge, although the equal protection attack on them was dismissed on standing and so remains formally unresolved.
relevance.FAIL-05: Because the equal protection challenge to ICWA's race-conscious placement preferences was dismissed for lack of standing rather than decided, counsel litigating discrimination in placement should treat that question as open rather than settled.

cases.holding: Both termination decrees were vacated: DCYF failed to make reasonable efforts as to the mother because it never offered substance-abuse treatment for what it identified as her primary barrier to reunification, and the father's unfitness was never proved by clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: due process requires that, before the state may terminate a parent's rights in his or her children, the state must support its allegations by clear and convincing evidence

relevance.OUT-02: Steven D. is the standard Rhode Island citation for the unfitness-first, clear-and-convincing rule, and it shows the Court vacating a decree where the trial justice made no unfitness findings at all as to one parent.
relevance.ACT-01: The case holds that a service plan is not a reasonable effort when it omits treatment for the very condition DCYF and its own expert identified as the principal barrier to reunification.
relevance.ACT-02: It is the Rhode Island decision most useful to a parent arguing that court-ordered services were misdirected, because the remedy was vacatur of the termination rather than deference to the department's choices.
relevance.OUT-05: The decree was vacated as to both parents and the matter returned to the Family Court, the disposition a Rhode Island parent seeks when the record will not carry the statutory ground.

cases.holding: Termination of the father's rights to Jazlyn was affirmed on the cruel-or-abusive-conduct ground, the Court holding that abuse of another child in the household, together with medical evidence of inflicted injury to Jazlyn, supported the finding.
cases.quote: cruel or abusive conduct towards one child in a household can serve as a basis for terminating a parent's rights with respect to another child in the household

relevance.FAIL-04: Jazlyn P., not In re Kristopher J., is the source authority for the rule that cruel or abusive conduct toward one child in the household supports termination as to the other children, and Kristopher J. quotes it for that proposition.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the Rhode Island decision establishing that catastrophic harm to one child in a household is the evidentiary foundation for protective action as to a surviving sibling.

cases.holding: The Family Court erred in dismissing the dependency-and-neglect petition as to Luz because evidence of harm to her sister Sonia was relevant to Luz's own status; both orders were vacated and the cases remanded for evidentiary hearings.
cases.quote: evidence of harm to one child of a family is relevant to the issues raised by a dependency-and-neglect petition regarding another child of the family

relevance.DEC-03: Luz J. is the origin of the Rhode Island sibling-evidence rule that In re King J. and In re Christina V. apply, and it is the authority to cite when a substantiation as to one child rests on proof about another.

cases.holding: Termination was affirmed because DCYF's case plans were targeted to the conduct that caused removal and the father refused to complete them, and the Court reiterated that DCYF need not show extraordinary efforts to reunite parent and child.
cases.quote: the services offered were patently targeted to address the reasons that Lauren and Stephanie were placed into care

relevance.ACT-01: Lauren B. is the current Rhode Island statement of what a voluntary or agency service plan must contain to qualify as reasonable efforts: services aimed at the actual reasons the children came into care.
relevance.ACT-02: It supplies the ceiling that In re Violet G. does not state expressly, because the Court confirms that extraordinary efforts are not required and that reasonable efforts are assessed case by case against the parent's own cooperation.
relevance.OUT-01: The opinion recognizes that reunification may be unattainable even when DCYF has made the requisite reasonable efforts, which is the rule that closes the reunification path in a non-compliant-parent case.

cases.holding: Termination was affirmed: a parent has no absolute right to be physically present at a termination hearing, and the voluntarily absent mother received due process because her attorney actively participated throughout.
cases.quote: the attorney unquestionably took an active role in the proceeding by his presence, his cross-examination of the opposing witness, and his closing argument

relevance.DEC-05: Ariel N. is the authority In re Julian D. relies on for how a Rhode Island dependency or termination case proceeds against an absent parent, and it identifies active participation by counsel as the specific safeguard that satisfies due process.

cases.case_name: Direct Action for Rights & Equality v. Gannon
cases.holding: The 1998 APRA amendments applied to the pending action, so attorneys' fees ran from the filing of the complaint and no knowing and willful violation had to be shown to award them, while redaction of complainants' Social Security numbers and officers' badge numbers was properly allowed.
cases.quote: the underlying policy of the APRA is the promotion of the free flow and disclosure of information to the public

relevance.FAIL-06: Gannon is the Rhode Island APRA decision applied throughout Providence Journal Co., and it is the authority that puts the statutory thumb on the scale toward disclosure before the privacy balancing begins.
relevance.PMC-05: It establishes both the pro-disclosure baseline and its practical limit, holding that unique personal identifiers may be redacted from otherwise releasable investigative records.
relevance.PMC-06: The fee-shifting holding is the enforcement lever for outside accountability work: a prevailing requester recovers fees from the date of the complaint without proving that the agency acted knowingly and willfully.

cases.case_name: Connor B. Ex Rel. Vigurs v. Patrick
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
cases.holding: Judgment on the record for the state child welfare defendants was affirmed because the foster children's class did not prove a substantial departure from accepted professional judgment under Youngberg, and class-wide liability is a precursor to any systemic injunctive relief.
cases.quote: Not only has class-wide liability not been shown, itself a needed precursor to any relief, but plaintiffs have also not met the requirements for injunctive relief.

relevance.INP-09: Connor B. shows what happens to a First Circuit systemic foster-care class action after it clears the standing and next-friend stage that Sam M. addresses, and it sets the merits standard such oversight litigation must meet.
relevance.ACT-03: The court held that placement and kinship decisions are matters of professional judgment, so a class attack on Rhode Island placement practice must show a substantial departure from accepted professional standards rather than poor outcomes.
relevance.FAIL-03: This is the First Circuit's most recent merits treatment of a claim that a state child welfare system fails federal and constitutional standards, and it explains why such claims rarely succeed even when performance data are poor.
relevance.PMC-01: The court expressly declined to treat a state's bottom-of-the-rankings performance on federal measures as evidence of a constitutional violation, which marks the limit of what CFSR-style data can prove in litigation.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
cases.holding: Dismissal of the section 1983 claims arising from the murder of a teenage state witness in Providence was affirmed because the state's unkept promises of protection did not deprive her of liberty, so neither the special-relationship nor the state-created-danger theory removed the case from DeShaney.
cases.quote: Merely alleging state actions which render the individual more vulnerable to harm, under a theory of state created danger, cannot be used as an end run around DeShaney's core holding.

relevance.FAIL-04: Rivera is the First Circuit's Rhode Island authority on the affirmative-duty exceptions to DeShaney, and it is the case J.R. v. Gloria builds on when it asks whether DCYF's relationship with a child creates a constitutional duty to protect.
relevance.OUT-06: When a child or youth is harmed after state actors knew of the danger but never took custody, Rivera is the decision that forecloses the damages claim absent a genuine deprivation of liberty.
relevance.PMC-04: Rivera demonstrates why after-the-fact review of a preventable death in Rhode Island is an administrative and legislative function: the constitutional tort route is closed unless the state restrained the victim's freedom to protect herself.

cases.holding: Termination of the non-Indian mother's rights to an Indian child was affirmed: ICWA applied, DCYF's efforts were active efforts, and the required qualified expert witness may be qualified in any relevant field where the case raises no culturally-relevant issues.
cases.quote: while at least one qualified expert witness is necessary under § 1912(f), that expert may be qualified in any relevant area if, as here, the case presents no culturally-relevant issues

relevance.INP-11: Roman A. is the second published Rhode Island ICWA decision and it qualifies In re Tamika R., holding that the qualified-expert-witness requirement survives but that the expert need not be an expert in Indian cultural affairs in a culturally neutral case.
relevance.ACT-02: The opinion is the Rhode Island Supreme Court's fullest description of what ICWA 'active efforts' demand of DCYF, a standard higher than the ordinary reasonable-efforts obligation in a court-ordered service plan.

notes: Court structure: Rhode Island has no intermediate appellate court. The Supreme Court of Rhode Island (CourtListener court_id 'ri') is the only appellate court, and abuse/neglect, dependency, termination, adoption and guardianship matters are tried in the Family Court, whose decisions are not published or carried on CourtListener. Every state case in this brief is therefore a published opinion of the state's highest court. No unpublished memorandum decisions were used.

All 37 cases were retrieved from the CourtListener API in this session and the full opinion text of each was read. Every quote was verified programmatically as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text (whitespace, curly quotes, dashes and the section symbol normalized), and every quote is from the majority/for-the-Court opinion, not a syllabus, headnote, dissent or concurrence.

Deliberate omission: Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000), is the case most often cited for the parental liberty interest, but its lead opinion is a four-Justice plurality rather than a majority, so it was excluded under the majority-only quoting rule. Stanley v. Illinois (majority) and Santosky v. Kramer (majority) supply the same propositions, and the First Circuit's Hatch opinion supplies the Rhode-Island-specific formulation.

Reporter citations: CourtListener's cluster records for In re Roman A. (2019) and In re Mandy M. (2020) carry no reporter citation, so both are given in slip form with docket number. Both are Published-status opinions of the Supreme Court of Rhode Island, not memoranda. Counsel should confirm the A.3d parallel cite before filing.

Gaps for which no published Rhode Island appellate authority could be located, despite targeted searches of court_id 'ri' and 'risuperct': (a) central-registry / administrative substantiation hearings and name-clearing due process -- DCYF substantiation appeals proceed administratively and then to the Superior Court, and no published appellate opinion on the due process content of that process was found; (b) extended foster care, Chafee services, or Family Court jurisdiction past age 18; (c) children missing or absent from foster care; (d) an express kinship or sibling placement preference; (e) formal differential response / alternative response; (f) race, religion or disability discrimination in placement decisions as such (In re Christopher B. on mental deficiency and In re Tamika R. on ICWA cultural-bias guidelines are the nearest analogues). For those nodes the federal standard (Suter, DeShaney, Stanley) and the closest Rhode Island authority were supplied.

ICWA: Rhode Island has no state ICWA statute. The two published Rhode Island Supreme Court ICWA decisions located are In re Tamika R., 973 A.2d 547 (R.I. 2009) (qualified expert witness requirement; vacatur for non-compliance) and In re Roman A. (R.I. 2019) (active efforts; who qualifies as a qualified expert witness). Both are included and should be read together.

Section 1983 / removal: Hatch v. Department for Children, Youth & Their Families, 274 F.3d 12 (1st Cir. 2001), is the controlling circuit authority for Rhode Island and adopts a reasonable-suspicion (not probable-cause) standard for warrantless temporary custody. Suboh v. District Attorney's Office, 298 F.3d 81 (1st Cir. 2002), adds the requirement of an adequate post-deprivation hearing within a reasonable time. Carter ex rel. Caleb O. v. Lindgren, 502 F.3d 26 (1st Cir. 2007), applies Hatch to actual DCYF officers. J.R. v. Gloria, 593 F.3d 73 (1st Cir. 2010), supplies the conscience-shocking standard for harm suffered in DCYF foster care and also confirms Rhode Island sovereign and qualified immunity defenses to the parallel state negligence claims.

Critical practice point for families and counsel: In re Madlyn B., 187 A.3d 1105 (R.I. 2018), holds that a parent who waives the Family Court Rule 15(c)(5) probable-cause hearing forfeits any Fourth/Fourteenth Amendment challenge to DCYF's seventy-two-hour hold. The constitutional objection to an emergency removal must be raised in the Family Court at that hearing or it is lost on appeal. In re Kyeshon J. applies the same raise-or-waive rule to adoption/termination grounds.

Two Rhode Island decisions show terminations being undone on grounds the agency did not anticipate: In re Joziah B., 207 A.3d 451 (R.I. 2019) (no § 15-7-9 sworn affidavit of the absent parent's whereabouts before notice by publication -- decree vacated), and In re Izabella G., 140 A.3d 146 (R.I. 2016) (termination resting on incarceration collapsed when the underlying convictions were vacated on Fourth Amendment grounds).

Reporter immunity caveat: R.I. Gen. Laws § 40-11-4 grants civil and criminal immunity to any person who participates in good faith in making a report. In Curtis v. State Department for Children & Their Families, 522 A.2d 203 (R.I. 1987), the Supreme Court expressly noted (footnote 4) that 'the precise scope of that immunity has not yet been determined by this court' and decided the case on the merits instead. That scope still appears to be undecided by the Rhode Island Supreme Court; Watterson v. Page, 987 F.2d 1 (1st Cir. 1993), is persuasive only, because it construes New Hampshire's reporting-immunity statute (its familial-integrity holding is binding First Circuit law).

Systemic oversight in Rhode Island runs through next-friend class litigation (Sam M. ex rel. Elliott v. Carcieri, 608 F.3d 77 (1st Cir. 2010); Danny B. ex rel. Elliott v. Raimondo, 784 F.3d 825 (1st Cir. 2015)) rather than through private enforcement of Title IV-E, which Suter v. Artist M., 503 U.S. 347 (1992), forecloses. That pairing is the reason the PMC-family and FAIL-03 nodes map to the same small set of cases.

Records and transparency: Rhode Island's Access to Public Records Act cases (Providence Journal Co., 136 A.3d 1168 (R.I. 2016); Pontarelli, 176 A.3d 472 (R.I. 2018)) supply the balancing and 'not a public record' analyses; In re Grand Jury Subpoena, 748 A.2d 821 (R.I. 2000), governs confidential health care and counseling records. No published Rhode Island appellate decision construing the confidentiality provisions of R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 40-11 specifically (DCYF investigative records) was located.

The pre-existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the RI node files are keyword-match noise repeated across all 42 files (In re J.R.; In re N.O.; In re B.M.; In re A.N.; In re C.R.; In re N.D.; In re N.B.; In re R.M.; In re Da Cruz; and In re CVS Health Corporation Securities Litigation, which is a securities case with no child-welfare content). None were retained. Several of those titles are genuine recent Rhode Island termination appeals, but they apply the standards already set by the leading cases included here and carry no reporter citation.

Missing (for a later pass): Lassiter v. Department of Social Services, 452 U.S. 18 (1981) — the controlling Supreme Court authority on appointed counsel in termination proceedings (no categorical right; case-by-case due process). The brief builds FAIL-01 on In re Bryce T. and In re Mandy M. without ever citing the federal decision both operate under. This is the most conspicuous omission in the brief.

Missing (for a later pass): 42 U.S.C. sec. 1320a-2 (the 1994 'Suter fix'), with Blessing v. Freestone, 520 U.S. 329 (1997), Gonzaga University v. Doe, 536 U.S. 273 (2002), and Health & Hospital Corp. of Marion County v. Talevski, 599 U.S. 166 (2023) — ten nodes rest on Suter alone. Congress partially abrogated Suter's reasoning by statute, and the enforceability question is now governed by the Blessing/Gonzaga/Talevski framework. Citing Suter as unqualified controlling law across INP-09, INP-11, DEC-01, DEC-06, ACT-01, OUT-04, FAIL-03, PMC-01, PMC-02 and PMC-03 without these is a serious gap.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Steven D., 23 A.3d 1138 (R.I. 2011) — the standard Rhode Island citation (quoted in In re Kristopher J. at 115 A.3d 965) that a finding of parental unfitness is 'the first [and] necessary step before any termination of parental rights can be initiated.' Belongs on OUT-02 alongside In re Destiney L.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Jazlyn P., 31 A.3d 1273 (R.I. 2011) — expressly quoted in In re Kristopher J. for the proposition that 'cruel or abusive conduct towards one child in a household can serve as a basis for terminating a parent's rights with respect to another child in the household.' This, not Kristopher J., is the source authority the brief attributes to Kristopher J. at FAIL-04 and OUT-06.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Luz J., 447 A.2d 1148 (R.I. 1982) — the origin of the rule that 'evidence of harm to one child of a family is relevant to the issues raised by a dependency-and-neglect petition regarding another child,' quoted in In re King J. and relied on in In re Christina V. Belongs on DEC-03.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Lauren B., 78 A.3d 752 (R.I. 2013) — quoted in In re Violet G. for the reasonable-efforts standard and for the limit that DCYF need not show 'extraordinary efforts.' It is the current statement of the standard the brief attributes to In re Brooklyn M. and In re Violet G. Belongs on ACT-01 and ACT-02.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Ariel N., 892 A.2d 80 (R.I. 2006) — the authority In re Julian D. relies on, holding an absent respondent's due process rights adequately protected where counsel 'unquestionably took an active role in the proceeding.' Belongs on DEC-05 with Julian D.

Missing (for a later pass): Direct Action for Rights & Equality v. Gannon, 819 A.2d 651 (R.I. 2003) — the Rhode Island APRA balancing authority applied throughout Providence Journal Co. (quoted there at 819 A.2d 662). A practitioner briefing FAIL-06 or PMC-05 would cite it alongside, not instead of, Providence Journal.

Missing (for a later pass): Rivera v. Rhode Island, 402 F.3d 27 (1st Cir. 2005) — the First Circuit's state-created-danger / DeShaney-exception decision arising out of Rhode Island, discussed in J.R. v. Gloria. It is the circuit authority on the affirmative-duty exceptions the brief describes at FAIL-04 but never cites.

Missing (for a later pass): Connor B. ex rel. Vigurs v. Patrick, 774 F.3d 45 (1st Cir. 2014) — the First Circuit's most recent treatment of a systemic foster-care class action on the merits. It belongs with Sam M. and Danny B. on INP-09 and FAIL-03, because it shows what happens to such suits after they survive the standing and next-friend stage.

Missing (for a later pass): Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl, 570 U.S. 637 (2013) — the Supreme Court's construction of ICWA sec. 1912(d) 'active efforts' and sec. 1912(f) 'continued custody,' directly implicated by In re Roman A.'s non-custodial-Indian-father posture. Neither Rhode Island ICWA node cites it.

Missing (for a later pass): Haaland v. Brackeen, 599 U.S. 255 (2023) — rejecting the constitutional challenges to ICWA. Any 2026 brief mapping INP-11 to ICWA should confirm the statute's current standing rather than leaving the reader with two Rhode Island decisions from 2009 and 2019.

Department of Social Servs. of Durham Cty., 452 U.S. 18 (1981) for FAIL-01: it is the federal constitutional floor under which In re Bryce T. and In re Mandy M. operate, holding there is no categorical right to appointed counsel in a termination case and that the question is decided case by case by the trial court.

Added Blessing v. Freestone, 520 U.S. 329 (1997) for INP-09, DEC-01, PMC-01 and PMC-02: it requires a section 1983 plaintiff to point to a specific rights-creating provision rather than to a state's overall 'substantial compliance' with a federal plan, which is exactly what a systemic or screen-out claim against DCYF tries to do.

Added Gonzaga University v. Doe, 536 U.S. 273 (2002) for DEC-06, OUT-04, FAIL-03 and PMC-03: it supplies the unambiguous-conferral test that now decides whether any IV-B/IV-E, Chafee or CAPTA plan requirement is privately enforceable, replacing the looser reading some courts had drawn from Blessing's three factors.

Added Health and Hospital Corporation of Marion Cty. v. Talevski, 599 U.S. 166 (2023) for INP-09, INP-11, DEC-01, DEC-06, ACT-01, OUT-04, FAIL-03, PMC-01, PMC-02 and PMC-03: it is the current controlling framework for all ten nodes that previously rested on Suter alone, and it confirms both that Spending Clause statutes can create section 1983-enforceable rights and that the bar for doing so is demanding.

Added Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl, 570 U.S. 637 (2013) for INP-11 and ACT-04: it construes ICWA section 1912(f) 'continued custody' and section 1912(d) 'active efforts' for the non-custodial Indian parent posture that In re Roman A. presents, and it limits the section 1915(a) placement preferences to cases in which a preferred party has actually sought to adopt.

Added Haaland v. Added In re Jazlyn P., 31 A.3d 1273 (R.I. 2011) for FAIL-04 and OUT-06: this, not In re Kristopher J., is the source authority for the rule that cruel or abusive conduct toward one child in a household supports termination as to another child in that household.

Added In re Luz J., 447 A.2d 1148 (R.I. 1982) for DEC-03: it is the origin of the Rhode Island rule, later applied in In re King J. and In re Christina V., that evidence of harm to one child of a family is relevant to a dependency-and-neglect petition concerning another child.

Added In re Lauren B., 78 A.3d 752 (R.I. 2013) for ACT-01, ACT-02 and OUT-01: it is the current Rhode Island statement of the reasonable-efforts standard, including the limits that services must target the reasons the children came into care, that extraordinary efforts are not required, and that reunification may be unattainable even when reasonable efforts were made.

Added In re Ariel N., 892 A.2d 80 (R.I. 2006) for DEC-05: it is the authority In re Julian D. relies on, holding that an absent parent's due process rights are adequately protected where counsel takes an active role in the proceeding.

Added Direct Action for Rights & Equality v. Gannon, 819 A.2d 651 (R.I. 2003) for FAIL-06, PMC-05 and PMC-06: it is the APRA decision applied throughout Providence Journal Co., it states the pro-disclosure baseline that precedes the privacy balancing, it permits redaction of unique personal identifiers, and its fee-shifting holding gives a prevailing requester fees from the date of the complaint without proof of a knowing and willful violation.

Added Connor B. ex rel. Vigurs v. Patrick, 774 F.3d 45 (1st Cir. 2014) for INP-09, ACT-03, FAIL-03 and PMC-01: it is the First Circuit's most recent merits treatment of a systemic foster-care class action and shows what such suits must prove -- a substantial departure from accepted professional judgment -- after they clear the standing and next-friend stage addressed in Sam M. Although the defendant agency was the Massachusetts DCF, the decision is binding First Circuit law in Rhode Island and the court expressly declined to treat bottom-of-the-rankings federal performance data as evidence of a constitutional violation.

Added Rivera v. Rhode Island, 402 F.3d 27 (1st Cir. 2005) for FAIL-04, OUT-06 and PMC-04: it is the First Circuit's Rhode Island decision on the DeShaney affirmative-duty exceptions, holding that a state-created-danger theory cannot substitute for the deprivation of liberty DeShaney requires; J.R. v. Gloria builds on it.

Added In re Roman A., No. 2017-113-Appeal. (R.I. Nov. 18, 2019) for INP-11 and ACT-02: the prior notes described this decision as included but no case entry existed, so the brief's ICWA coverage was in fact a single 2009 case. COULD NOT VERIFY AS A CASE: 42 U.S.C. sec. 1320a-2 (the 1994 'Suter fix', Pub. L. 103-432). This is a statute, not a judicial decision, and CourtListener's opinion database therefore cannot be used to verify it. No case entry was created for it. Counsel should read the statutory text directly; its effect is that a provision of the Social Security Act is not to be deemed unenforceable merely because the State plan is required to contain it, while leaving intact Suter's actual holding on 42 U.S.C. sec. 671(a)(15). The judicial framework that now governs the enforceability question is supplied here by Blessing, Gonzaga and Talevski, all three of which were retrieved and read in this session.
